title: Review of Sentencing Framework for Sexual and Hurt Offences
what_it_is: Review of Sentencing Framework for Sexual and Hurt Offences

sections.label: Protection of women discussion
sections.summary: The discussion on protection of women is timely, following cases of sexual and hurt offences and a broad-based conversation on women's position in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Our discussion today on protection of women is timely.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: We have had some cases for the past few years relating to sexual and hurt offences which triggered much discussion on whether the sentences imposed were adequate.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: In September 2020, last year, we started off an important broad-based conversation on the position of women in Singapore, how we can better deal with the issues they face, not just crimes but the overall position of women.

sections.label: Broad-based review of women
sections.summary: The review will look into ingraining equality and respect for women, changing mindsets and attitudes, with a White Paper due later this year.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The broad-based review will look into how equality and respect for women can be better ingrained in our society and inculcated as a fundamental value from young; and to change mindsets, tackle underlying attitudes and behavioural patterns.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: We have had many discussions with various groups, many more discussions are planned and we are on track to issue the White Paper later this year.

sections.label: Probation sentence and High Court
sections.summary: The Court gave 21 months probation, but the High Court agreed with the AGC and imposed two weeks imprisonment.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The Court gave him 21 months of probation.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The probation report stated, and I quote, "good academic performance in school, highlighted his potential to excel in life".

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: They did not agree that a sentence of probation was appropriate and the High Court agreed with the AGC and imposed two weeks imprisonment.

sections.label: Amended Penal Code and POHA
sections.summary: In 2019, the Penal Code and Protection from Harassment Act were amended to give enhanced penalties for offences against vulnerable victims, up to twice the maximum punishment.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: In 2019, we amended the Penal Code and Protection from Harassment Act, or POHA.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Under the amended provisions, those who commit sexual and hurt offences against vulnerable victims, face enhanced penalties.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Offenders who commit offences against such vulnerable victims are now liable for up to twice the maximum prescribed punishment.

sections.label: Increased hurt penalty and effective date
sections.summary: Maximum penalty for voluntarily causing hurt increased from two to three years imprisonment, with both amendments taking effect on 1 January 2020.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Maximum penalty for voluntarily causing hurt has been increased from two to three years imprisonment.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Both the penal code and POHA amendments took effect on 1 January 2020 and the amendments apply to offences committed on or after that date.

sections.label: Increased imprisonment terms for offences
sections.summary: Maximum imprisonment term will increase from two to three years, and for similar offences involving sexual communication with minors, from one to two years.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We want egregious cases to be dealt with more severely.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We will increase the maximum imprisonment term from two years, to three years.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: These two offences are similar in nature to offences involving sexual communication with minors.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We will therefore correlate the penalties – increase the maximum sentence from one year to two years’ imprisonment.

sections.label: AGC objects to rehabilitative sentences
sections.summary: AGC agrees it will generally object to probation and community-based sentences for adults committing certain hurt or sexual offences.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I have discussed this with AGC and AGC agrees with our view.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Therefore, AGC will generally object to rehabilitative sentences, such as probation and community-based sentences, where the offenders are adults who commit certain types of hurt or sexual offences.

sections.label: Sentencing Advisory Panel set up
sections.summary: MHA and MinLaw discussed with stakeholders including AGC and the Judiciary, and will set up a Panel issuing non-binding sentencing guidelines.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: MHA and MinLaw have discussed with various stakeholders, including AGC, the Judiciary.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We will set up a Sentencing Advisory Panel.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The key function of the Panel will be to issue non-binding sentencing guidelines.

sections.label: April 2020 probation overturned
sections.summary: The view is that the High Court's April 2020 overturning of probation for imprisonment was appropriate and would be so now.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The first case, the one in April 2020, where the High Court overturned the initial sentence of probation and imposed imprisonment, our view is that that was appropriate and that would be the case now with the amendments.

sections.label: Hurt in intimate relationship penalty
sections.summary: Acts after 1 January 2020 would likely be charged under new Penal Code provisions, with up to six years' jail, $10,000 fine, or both.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Had the acts been committed on or after 1 January 2020, he is likely to have been charged under the new Penal Code provisions, voluntarily causing hurt to a victim with whom he was in an intimate or close relationship.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: For voluntarily causing hurt, twice the maximum penalty is up to six years’ jail, $10,000 fine, or both.

sections.label: Voyeurism offence and penalties
sections.summary: Voyeurism now carries double the penalty of two years' jail or fine, plus possible caning, and AGC will generally object to probation or community-based sentences.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Before the Penal Code amendments came into force in 2020, such acts were usually prosecuted under the rubric of insulting the modesty of a woman, punishable with up to one year’s imprisonment, or fine or both.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Now, with the introduction of a specific offence of voyeurism which carries double the penalty – two years’ jail, or fine – there is now also the possibility of caning.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: As I said, AGC will also, in general, object to probation or community-based sentences being imposed in cases involving voyeurism offences.

sections.label: Police handling of VCH offences
sections.summary: A Member asks whether the Ministry has considered handling non-arrestable voluntarily causing hurt offences more variatedly for expedited action in appropriate cases.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: There was a discussion amongst Members of how voluntarily causing hurt, being a non-arrestable offence, is dealt with by the Police.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Then-Senior Parliamentary Secretary who at the round-up speech confirmed that Police do look at voluntarily causing hurt (VCH) offences in some broad classes – I do not think those were closed classes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary then in the round-up speech mentioned that, I will quote what he said, "post-amendment we can assess if there is a need to create a more expedited framework for the resolution of other types of VCH cases and if this can be done without compromising due process or compromising the delivery of Police response to other more serious offences".

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: I would just like to confirm whether the Ministry has considered looking at VCH offences, the section 321 type of offences, the non-arrestable offences, in a more variated manner so that we can take expedited action in the appropriate cases.

sections.label: Feeling safe walking streets
sections.summary: The speaker says his position to the Police is that in such cases people want to walk the streets feeling safe.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: My position to the Police has been that those sorts of cases, you want to be able to walk in the streets, feeling safe.

sections.label: Enhancing penalties for position of trust
sections.summary: The question asks whether the Ministry would enhance the sentencing framework and increase penalties for offenders who start from a position of trust.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: Would the Ministry consider further enhancing the sentencing framework and increase the penalties for those who not only cause hurt or sexually abuse the victim, but start out from a position of trust, so that we ensure that such crimes where the victim already feels a sense of comfort in the presence of the person, does not fall prey to such offences.

sections.label: Courts treat position of trust seriously
sections.summary: The passage states that teachers and doctors in fiduciary relationships who take advantage are treated very seriously by the Courts in sentencing.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: If you are in a position of trust, if you are a teacher, that is a very serious consideration that is taken into account in sentencing.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, there will be no question in the minds of people, if you are a teacher, if you are a doctor, you are in a position of fiduciary relationship where you have control or you have oversight over the other person and you take advantage, the Courts treat that very seriously, and we have reflected that approach quite clearly.

sections.label: Professional and criminal consequences
sections.summary: The passage states that offenders face professional and criminal consequences, and that being in a position of trust is central to enhancing penalties.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, you will face both professional consequences and criminal consequences.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, I think we ought to be quite clear that being in a position of trust is a very material – in fact, central – consideration in enhancing penalties.

sections.label: Enhanced penalties for domestic worker offences
sections.summary: Section 73 provides enhanced penalties for offences against domestic workers, which can be twice the maximum penalty.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: At section 73, it says that there are enhanced penalties for offences against domestic workers, and that can be twice the maximum penalty.

sections.label: Protection for intimate partner relationships
sections.summary: Protection was extended to persons in an intimate partner relationship, so abusing a girlfriend brings enhanced penalties and POHA orders.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, we extended the protection to persons in an intimate partner relationship.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, if you abuse your girlfriend, now these enhanced penalties will apply to you, and your girlfriend can take out the appropriate orders under POHA, for example.

sections.label: Prosecution objection to community sentencing
sections.summary: The prosecution generally objects to community-based or rehab-based sentencing for sexual and hurt offences, focusing on deterrence, and AGC will be clearer hereafter.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: On the first question that AG, AGC or prosecution will generally object in general, in fact, as I have said in my speech, for some time now, that has been the position of prosecution in general when it comes to sexual and hurt offences.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: They object to community-based sentencing or rehab-based sentencing, and they focus on deterrence and sending the message.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I am re-emphasising and reaffirming that approach and saying that AGC will be even clearer in that approach hereafter.

sections.label: Deterrence and prevention as considerations
sections.summary: Deterrence, prevention and sending a clear message will be the primary considerations, as a fundamental tenet and value.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The primary considerations will be deterrence and prevention and sending the message clearly, and consistent with what I have articulated, as a fundamental tenet and value.

sections.label: Sentencing Advisory Panel remit
sections.summary: The Sentencing Advisory Panel's remit is being worked out and is intended to cover beyond sexual and hurt offences.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: On the Sentencing Advisory Panel, the remit is being worked out.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I think it makes sense for the remit to be covering beyond sexual and hurt offences, and that is the intention.

sections.label: Court sentence and AGC assessment
sections.summary: The Courts imposed a sentence in line with precedents then, and AGC assessed it would not be easy to challenge.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The Courts imposed a sentence that was in line with the precedents at that point in time and AGC's assessment was that it was not going to be easy to challenge.

sections.label: Trauma literacy training question
sections.summary: The question asks whether the Government will consider programmes and training for trauma literacy in the criminal justice system to safeguard victims.

sentences.speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Other than the intention to amend the maximum penalties for three sexual offences, will the Government consider putting in place programmes and training to better ensure trauma literacy within the criminal justice system to safeguard the interest of victims of hurt and sexual offences?

sections.label: Balancing deterrence and rehabilitation
sections.summary: The question asks how deterrence and rehabilitation are balanced, which offences exclude rehabilitation, and how the public and youths are educated on consent.

sentences.speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: I know that some offenders pay for a very long time, beyond their sentence, and society includes them too.

sentences.speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: I hope the Minister can elaborate more about how the sentencing principles of deterrence and rehabilitation to prevent future incidence of reoffending are balanced in the second proposal as the range of sexual and hurt offences is very wide.

sentences.speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: What do certain offences where rehabilitation will not be considered include?

sentences.speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: What steps are being taken to educate the public and, in particular, youths about consent and power dynamics in sexual interactions and what role can the media and public more responsibly play to elevate the conversation?

sentences.speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: I appreciate the sentencing guideline and just hope that it can be made friendly to the layman so that it is easily disseminated, for example, by social media.

sections.label: Protecting victims in court
sections.summary: Victims' interests can be submitted to Courts, gag orders can protect identity, and video-recorded interviews are being explored as evidence.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: With that, how do we take into account victims' interests and protect them?

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: They can be submitted to the Courts so that the Courts are very informed about the impact of the offence on the victim, and the emotional and physical trauma that has been suffered.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: In order to protect the identity of the alleged victim, gag orders can be made.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I have given you in my Ministerial Statement a framework in such cases on how the victim could be protected from some types of cross examination, from having to face the accused, from having screens to protect them.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Of course, in addition, there are Protection Orders available and Expedited Protection Orders available under the Protection from Harassment Act (POHA) and the Women's Charter, as appropriate.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We are also exploring, we are talking to the Courts about the possibility of recording video-recorded interviews of victims and then, using those videos as evidence in court in lieu of examination-in-chief.

sections.label: Imprisonment and caning for offences
sections.summary: Courts may impose imprisonment and caning instead of rehabilitative sentences due to offence nature, severity and risk of recurrence.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The Courts may impose imprisonment and caning instead of a rehabilitative sentence like probation or reformative training, because of the nature of the offence, its severity and the likelihood or the possibility that this may happen again and other people need to be protected.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: For adult offenders, I have explained, for sexual and hurt offences, rehabilitation would not be the dominant consideration unless there is a strong propensity to reform and specific factors strongly point to rehabilitation.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But I have also said, "I am a person with bright prospects" or "I am an undergraduate who is going to do well in life" – those are not very relevant factors.

sections.label: Panel views and Australia comparison
sections.summary: Consideration will be given to whether the panel can be invited to give views, though Singapore differs from Australia.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: On Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim's two questions, and as to whether the panel can be invited to give views, we will give consideration but the situation in Singapore is slightly different from Australia.

sections.label: Sentencing guideline persuasiveness
sections.summary: A sentencing guideline issued by such a body would be highly persuasive.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: A sentencing guideline issued by such a body, would be as I said, highly persuasive.

sections.label: Panel size and diversity
sections.summary: The panel will not be very large, with limits on numbers, and diversity should not be a primary goal.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: By necessity, the panel will not be a very large panel and there will be limits on how many people can be there.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: There is, in principle, no disability imposed on people, but I do not think we should run after this with diversity as a primary goal.

sections.label: Panel guidelines and judicial independence
sections.summary: Non-binding panel guidelines could pressure Courts to explain deviations, raising concern about Executive intrusion into sentencing and judicial independence.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: While it says that this panel's decisions will not be binding on the Court, it does create a situation, if the Courts were to deviate from the guidelines issued by this panel, it does create a situation that requires an explanation and therefore could create some pressure.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: So, my question is, how does the Minister address the concern that this could be viewed as the Executive arm going into an area that has traditionally been under the Judiciary, and could this potentially compromise the independence of the Judiciary in the area of sentencing?

sections.label: Maximum penalty for offence
sections.summary: The law sets out maximum penalties of four years and five years for such an offence.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The law sets out maximum penalty – four years, five years – for such an offence.

sections.label: Sentencing Advisory Panel role
sections.summary: A Sentencing Advisory Panel can flesh out non-binding guidance for certain cases, and more than half its members will be judges.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: And the Second Reading speech tries to flesh it out a bit more.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But a Sentencing Advisory Panel looking at different types of cases can set out, flesh out a little bit more, in non-binding language in cases that fall into this sort of factual matrix involving offenders above a certain age, involving this type of offence.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: That is what the Sentencing Advisory Panel can do.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: And as I indicated, more than half of the Sentencing Advisory Panel will comprise judges anyway.

sections.label: Workplace sexual harassment survey
sections.summary: An AWARE-Ipsos survey found 40% of Singapore workers reported workplace sexual harassment, but only three in 10 officially reported it.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: An AWARE-Ipsos survey in November found that 40% of workers in Singapore said they had been sexually harassed at the workplace, but only three in 10 of them officially reported it, for reasons that include the fear of not being believed or being blamed for bringing it upon themselves.

sections.label: Advisory and POHA limits
sections.summary: The measure is only advisory and not statutory, and POHA requires victims to file a court order that may be onerous.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: However, it is only an advisory and it is not a statutory requirement.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: I also understand that we have POHA, but that requires the victim to file for a court order which may be too onerous for them.

sections.label: Easier protection order applications
sections.summary: POHA was amended to allow expedited orders, make orders easier to obtain, and criminalise continuous breaches of Protection Orders.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: It has been made relatively easy to apply and get such orders.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We amended POHA to make expedited orders possible and make it even easier for orders to be obtained and we also made it criminal if people continuously breached Protection Orders.

sections.label: MinLaw review of applications
sections.summary: MinLaw was asked to analyse the number of applications, time taken, effectiveness of the process, and possible improvements.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: One of the remits I have asked MinLaw to look at would be, has been to analyse the number of applications that have been made, the time that has been taken and how effective is the process, and whether there are things that can be done to make it more effective.

sections.label: Exposure of children to sexual images
sections.summary: Exposing young children to sexual images is an offence and the penalties have been enhanced.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: On the exposure of young children to sexual images, that is an offence.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I talked about it and, in fact, the penalties have been enhanced.

sections.label: Multi-agency effort through schools
sections.summary: A multi-agency effort is being done through conversations and schools to instil this approach from when people are young.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: That is the approach we have to instil.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, it has got to bring a multi-agency effort to the table and that is what is being done through the conversations, understanding we have got to do it in the schools, we have got to get people to understand, we have to get them to understand from the time they are young.
